sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Toxicity: CNS/respiratory depression, hypotonia, coma, bradycardia from excess baclofen; Withdrawal: severe spasticity, seizures, autonomic instability — intrathecal baclofen withdrawal mimics malignant hyperthermia and can be fatal
TOXICITY findings
--CNS depression**: somnolence: coma. With large intoxications, brainstem reflexes may lost (mimics brain death)
--Hypothermia, ↓ HR, ↓ BP (lowdose). Paradoxical HTN/tachycardia with >200mg
--Hypotonia, flaccid paralysis, absent reflexes
--Respiratory depression: rate, depth, SpO2
--Excessive salivation, nystagmus, myoclonus
WITHDRAWAL findings
--Rebound spasticity: rigidity, hyperreflexia, clonus, hypertonia
--Autonomic instability: tachycardia, HTN or ↓ BP, hyperthermia
--Agitation, hallucinations, delirium, disorientation, seizures
--Diaphoresis, goosebumps, pruritus
--Resembles NMS: rigidity + fever + tachycardia + AMS + autonomic instability
--Pump site: inspect for infection, swelling, catheter displacement

pairs.value: Intentional or accidental. Risk factors: renal impairment, concurrent CNS depressants, dose escalation
Pump delivers excessive bolus: ascending flaccid paralysis, respiratory arrest
AKI or CKD progression without dose adjustment. Check GFR
Battery depletion, reservoir empty, catheter fracture/kink, dosing error
Fever, AMS, hemodynamic instability: always check for infection, esp infected pump
Rigidity, fever, AMS, autonomic instability: check antipsychotic exposure, CK
Clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, diaphoresis: check serotonergic meds
Rigidity + hyperthermia postanesthesia: dantrolene is definitive tx
In spinal cord injury pts: HTN, ↓ HR, flushing above lesion
Tremor, agitation, seizures, tachycardia: Hx. of alcohol or benzo use

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Orders:** IV access, continuous SpO2, continuous EEG (withdrawal seizures), telemetry, toxicology/poison control consult
-**Labs:** BMP, CBC, ABG/VBG (if respiratory compromise), urine drug screen, baclofen level (if available)
**BMP with Cr/GFR:** Critical: renal function determines baclofen clearance & toxicity risk
**CK / myoglobin:** Rhabdo from severe spasticity/rigidity in withdrawal: causes AKI
**CBC, BCxs, lactate:** r/o sepsis: infected pump is an important ddx
**LFTs:** Baseline liver Fxn; dantrolene is hepatotoxic
**ABG/VBG:** Respiratory status in toxicity; acidosis in Rhabdo
**EEG:** For comatose pts with toxicity: nonconvulsive status epilepticus occurs
**Plain radiographs (KUB/spine):** Check catheter: kinking, migration, disconnection, fracture
**CT/MRI spine or contrast study:** If radiographs inconclusive: catheter tip position, CSF flow study
BACLOFEN TOXICITY (OD)
--Stop baclofen now: for pump pts, consult pump specialist & stop for 48h
--EEG monitoring: nonconvulsive status epilepticus can occur in comatose pts
--Hemodialysis: consider if severe renal failure + critical intoxication; NOT suggested with preserved renal function. Multiple sessionsneeded
--Must eventually restart baclofen at lower dose to prevent withdrawal
INTRACAL BACLOFEN WITHDRAWAL
--Resume intracal baclofen asas possible: this is only definitive tx
--Consult neurosurgery/anesthesia for pump revision or temporary lumbar drain
--Single IT bolus via lumbar puncture as temporizing bridge
--If IT access unavailable: multimodal oral therapy (see meds below)
--Aggressive supportive care: IV fluids, cooling for hyperthermia, Rhabdo management
ORAL BACLOFEN WITHDRAWAL
--Resume oral baclofen: definitive therapy, but resolution delayed up to 4 days (slow CNS penetration)
--Benzodiazepines + dexmedetomidine for agitation & autonomic instability
TOXICITY
--Monitor respiratory & neurological status closely: toxicity can last days with renal impairment
--Baclofen must be restarted at lower dose once toxicity resolving: abrupt discontinuation causes withdrawal
--If hemodialysis performed: multiple sessionsneeded. Goal is reduce baclofen enough for extubation: avoid excessive removal triggering withdrawal
--Serial CK if Rhabdo suspected; aggressive IV fluids to prevent renal injury
WITHDRAWAL
--Multimodal therapy is essential: no single agent adequately treats IT withdrawal. Use several antispasmodics at low doses for synergistic effect
--Preferred combination: oral baclofen + benzodiazepine + dexmedetomidine + tizanidine
--Strongest indication for intubation: profound hyperthermia: chemical paralysis eliminates skeletal muscle heat generation
--Aggressive cooling: target normothermia. Rhabdo management: IV NS, target UOP >200 mL/h
--Definitive: restore intracal delivery via pump revision or temporary lumbar drain
--Monitor CK q6-12h, renal function daily, telemetry
**Pump interrogation:** Consult pump specialist: check reservoir volume, battery, alarm Hx., programmed dose

drugs.name: Oral baclofen (for withdrawal)
drugs.dose: 10-20mg PO q8h
drugs.notes: Cannot fully treat IT withdrawal with oral baclofen: downregulated spinal GABAB receptors limit effectiveness. Slow onset (3-4 days). Use as part of multimodal approach.

drugs.name: Lorazepam (for withdrawal)
drugs.dose: 1-2mg IV q6h
drugs.notes: Stimulates spinal GABAA receptors: may circumvent GABAB deficiency. ↓ seizure risk. Titrate IV while observing response; hold if somnolence.

drugs.name: Midazolam (for withdrawal)
drugs.dose: 1-4mg IV q6h
drugs.notes: Alternative benzodiazepine. Shorter acting than lorazepam. No optimal dosing data: titrate to effect.

drugs.name: Diazepam (for withdrawal)
drugs.dose: 2-10mg IV q6h PRN
drugs.notes: Long halflife (20-50h): accumulates. May be useful for sustained coverage but monitor for oversedation.

drugs.name: Dexmedetomidine (for withdrawal)
drugs.dose: 0.2-1.5 mcg/kg/h IV infusion
drugs.notes: Preferred for agitation: highly titratable, does NOT cause respiratory suppression. Suppresses sympathetic activation (tachycardia, HTN).

drugs.name: Tizanidine (for withdrawal)
drugs.dose: 4mg PO q8h
drugs.notes: Oral alpha2 agonist with greater antispasmodic activity & less sedation than dexmedetomidine. Adjunct for spasticity.

drugs.name: Cyproheptadine (for withdrawal)
drugs.dose: 4mg PO q6h, uptitrate to 8mg q6h
drugs.notes: Antihistamine with antiserotonergic & antispasmodic properties. Sedative. Reasonable adjunct in multimodal approach.

drugs.name: Dantrolene (secondline for withdrawal)
drugs.dose: 25mg PO daily, gradual uptitration
drugs.notes: Ryanodine receptor antagonist: acts directly on skeletal muscle. Role unclear; save for refractory spasticity.

drugs.name: Propofol (rescue for withdrawal)
drugs.dose: Intubation + 25-80 mcg/kg/min IV infusion
drugs.notes: Rescue thetherapy: for refractory rigidity or extreme hyperthermia when other agents fail. Requires intubation. Chemical paralysis may needed.

pairs.value: GABAB receptor agonist used for spasticity (oral or intracal pump). Narrow therapeutic window, esp with renal impairment
OD or accumulation causing CNS depression, respiratory failure, seizures, & hemodynamic instability. Ingestion >200-400mg associated with coma, seizure, or intubation
Lifethreatening cessation of IT baclofen from pump malfunction, catheter fracture, battery/reservoir depletion, or dosing error. More severe than oral withdrawal
Agitated delirium, seizures, autonomic instability within 1-4 days of stopping. Slower onset than IT withdrawal
Peak plasma 2-3h postingestion. Halflife 4-5h (nl. renal function). CSF penetration is slow: clinical effects begin 3-4 days, peak 5-10 days
GFR <30 is strong contraindication. GFR 50-80: reduce dose 33%. GFR 30-50: reduce dose 50%. Accumulation causes toxicity

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Hyperthermia + generalized muscle rigidity + hypercarbia triggered by volatile anesthetics (halothane, sevoflurane) or succinylcholine in genetically susceptible patients; rapidly fatal without dantrolene — call MH hotline immediately
Earliest signs: rising EtCO2, tachycardia, unexplained hypercarbia despite increased ventilation
Muscle rigidity, masseter spasm, generalized contracture,rising core temperature
Dark urine or myoglobinuria, signs of rhabdomyolysis, metabolic instability
Dysrhythmias, ↓ BP or hemodynamic collapse late in course
Hyperthermia may later sign —don't wait for high temperature to treat

pairs.value: Volatile anesthetics & succinylcholine are classic triggers
CK >20,000 c/w MH; +30 min delay in treatment increases complication risk
Hours to days after dopamine blockade, leadpipe rigidity, not tied to anesthesia exposure
Clonus & hyperreflexia with serotonergic exposure not anesthetic triggered rigidity

pairs.key: DDx: Sepsis / thyroid storm / heat injury
pairs.value: Can cause hyperthermia & tachycardia, but does not explain the classic anesthesia triggered hypercarbia & rigidity pattern

sections.title: Management
items: Call anesthesia & give **dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV**; repeat q5min until controlled,>10 mg/kg total
**Hyperventilate with 100% O2** & stop all triggering agents
**Treat complications**: bicarb for acidosis, standard txt for ↑K, & treat dysrhythmias by correcting acidosis/↑K first
Cool aggressively with ice, cooling blanket, & cold IV fluids; stop active cooling once temp reaches 38°C
Monitor for Rhabdo / recrudescence & continue ICUlevel care for 24-48h
Core temp: monitoring, target <38°C
**EtCO2 & ABG**: check CO2 clearance
CK q4-6h: peak may not occur until 12-24h after episode
Urine output & color: target UO **>1 mL/kg/hr**; dark urine = myoglobinuria
Electrolytes (K, Ca, Mg): ↑K is common
Coags: DIC can develop
Glucose q1h if insulin was given for ↑K
Recurrance possible (25% rate) after 24-48 hours

drugs.name: Dantrolene
drugs.dose: 2.5 mg/kg IV push, repeat q5min until resolved
drugs.contraindications: Hepatic impairment (relative — use in MH regardless); respiratory depression
drugs.notes: **First-line & only effective tx for MH.** May need >10 mg/kg acutely. Follow with 1 mg/kg q46h for 24-48h. Call MHAUS: 1-800-644-9737.

drugs.name: Sodium bicarb
drugs.dose: 12 mEq/kg IV
drugs.notes: For metabolic acidosis temporization if blood gas not yet available. Titrate to ABG.

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate
drugs.dose: 2-3g IV
drugs.contraindications: Digitalis toxicity (relative — may precipitate arrhythmia); hypercalcemia
drugs.notes: For ↑K: cardiac toxicity. **AVOID CCBs** (verapamil, diltiazem): cardiac arrest risk with dantrolene.

drugs.name: Regular insulin + Dextrose
drugs.dose: 10 units Insulin IV + D50 1 amp
drugs.notes: ↑K tx. check glucose q1h after administration.

drugs.name: **Cold** IV fluids
drugs.dose: Cold NS or LR wide open
drugs.contraindications: None in MH context; avoid in already-hypothermic patients
drugs.notes: Active cooling. Target temp <38°C (100.4°F). Stop active cooling at 38°C to avoid overshoot hypothermia.

pairs.value: Pharmacogenetic hypermetabolic crisis of skeletal muscle triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine
Rising EtCO2 / hypercarbia is first detectable sign
Muscle rigidity +rising temperature + tachycardia shortly after anesthesia induction
Recurrence after initial txt occurs in ~25% of cases: watch for 2448h

items: Occupation: farming, pesticide application, industrial chemical exposure
Exposure type: organophosphate insecticide, carbamate, nerve agent
Route: dermal, ingestion, inhalation
Time since exposure: determines likelihood of enzyme aging
Intentional vs accidental: suicide attempt common in developing countries

Prehospital tx: was atropine given? How much?
Coexposures: solvents, or pesticides

pairs.value: SLUDGE (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis) + DUMBELS + miosis + bronchospasm + bradycardia from organophosphates, nerve agents, or physostigmine; bronchospasm and secretions kill — atropine first
HR variable (↓ HR from muscarinic, tachycardia from nicotinic); BP ↑ or variable; RR ↑; temp nl. or ↓
Miosis (pinpoint): classic muscarinic finding
Bronchorrhea (copious secretions), bronchospasm, wheezing, ↑ WOB: primary cause of death
Diaphoresis: profuse sweating; may see chemical odor (garliclike with organophosphates)
Hyperactive bowel sounds, cramping, diarrhea, emesis, salivation
Fasciculations (nicotinic), weakness, AMS, seizures
Urinary incontinence
Lacrimation, miosis, blurred vision
Malathion, parathion, chlorpyrifos, diazinon: agricultural insecticides
Sarin, soman, tabun, VX, Novichok: chemical warfare agents
Aldicarb, carbaryl: similar presentation but reversible (no aging); 2PAM still indicated
Neostigmine, pyridostigmine, edrophonium, echothiophate: cholinesterase inhibitors
Inocybe, Clitocybe species: muscarinic sx without nicotinic effects
Opioid toxicity (miosis but no secretions/fasciculations), nicotine toxicity, serotonin syndrome (more diaphoresis/clonus)

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** POC glucose,BMP, CBC(leukocytosis), !!RBC cholinesterase + plasma cholinesterase!!, ABG/VBG (resp failure, acidosis assessment)
-**Orders:** IV access, continuous SpO2, **EKG**(QTc prolongation correlates with severity) atropine at bedside, pralidoxime (2-PAM) at bedside, decontamination  toxicology/poison control consult
Ensure Decontaminated
Ensure Airway patient, hemodynamically stable
cardiac monitoring, pulse oximetry, IV access
Give **atropine 2 mg IV** & increase dose q3-5 min until pulmonary secretions dry
--**Atropine gtt**: once secretions controlled, start infusion at 10-20% of total loading dose per hour
Add pralidoxime (2PAM) 1-2 g IV over 15-30 min, then infusion if needed; give early before enzyme aging
--2PAM is most effective within first 24-48 hrs but may still help later —don't withhold based on time alone
Treat seizures/agitation with benzos & support airway/ventilation as needed
--RBC acetylcholinesterase (confirmatory but results delayed)
--Plasma butyrylcholinesterase / pseudocholinesterase (faster but less specific)
**CXR**: pulmonary edema in severe cases
!!Nicotinic effects!! (tachycardia, HTN, mydriasis) can mask classic muscarinic presentation: **Don't R/O dx based on absence of miosis**
Watch for !!intermediate syndrome!!: proximal weakness & resp failure at 24-96 hrs
Lipophilic agents (fenthion, chlorfenthion) --> delayed/prolonged toxicity: watch 24+ hrs
Avoid succinylcholine for RSI: depressed pseudocholinesterase causes prolonged paralysis; use !!rocuronium!!

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.dose: 2 mg IV; double dose q3-5 min until secretions dry; may need 10-100+ mg/24h
drugs.notes: Titrate to drying of pulmonary secretions: NOT pupil size. Start infusion once stabilized (10-20% of loading dose/hr)

drugs.name: Pralidoxime (2PAM)
drugs.dose: 1-2 g IV over 15-30 min, then 500 mg/hr infusion; peds: 20-50 mg/kg, then 5-10 mg/kg/hr
drugs.notes: Give ASAP: must give before aging occurs. Reverses nicotinic effects (weakness, fasciculations). Continue infusion ≥24 hrs

drugs.name: Diazepam
drugs.dose: 5-10 mg IV; peds 0.2-0.5 mg/kg
drugs.notes: For seizures: organophosphate seizures are cholinergic, not epileptic; benzos are first line

drugs.name: Glycopyrrolate
drugs.notes: Alternative to atropine for peripheral muscarinic sx only; does NOT treat CNS effects or seizures

pairs.value: **S**alivation, **L**acrimation, **U**rination, **D**iarrhea, **G**I cramping, **E**mesis, **M**iosis: muscarinic effects mnemonic
**D**iarrhea/**D**iaphoresis, **U**rination, **M**iosis, **B**radycardia/**B**ronchorrhea/**B**ronchospasm, **E**mesis, **L**acrimation, **S**alivation
Mydriasis, tachycardia, weakness, fasciculations, HTN: can mask classic muscarinic presentation
Irreversible binding of organophosphate to acetylcholinesterase: once aged, 2PAM is ineffective; timing varies by agent
Proximal muscle weakness & respiratory failure occurring 24-96 hrs postexposure; monitor 48-96 hrs after severe exposure

Mydriasis: dilated, nonreactive; may delayed 12-24 hrs

Delirium, agitation, hallucinations: "mad as hatter"; dysarthria, mumbling, picking at air
Decreased/absent bowel sounds, ileus. obstruction if severe
Urinary retention: "full as flask"
Sinus tachycardia; if QRS wide: suspect TCA
Anticholinergic = DRY skin vs sympathomimetic = WET (diaphoretic). Both have mydriasis + tachycardia
Diphenhydramine (most common), hydroxyzine, promethazine, doxylamine
Amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine, desipramine: most dangerous (sodium channel blockade + seizures)

Cyclobenzaprine (structurally similar to TCA), orphenadrine
Oxybutynin, tolterodine, hyoscyamine
Benztropine, trihexyphenidyl

**Check ECG**: if QRS >100 ms, give sodium bicarbonate 2 mEq/kg IV & treat as possible TCA toxicity, especially if taking
**Use benzos for agitation & start active cooling for hyperthermia**
Treat retention/supportive issues: Foley for urinary retention, IVF PRN, serial temp/ECG monitoring
**physostigmine 0.5-1 mg IV slow** only if no C/F TCA OD, no wide QRS, no seizure hx, & no brady/AV block
**--If physostigmine causes seizures: benzos will be INEFFECTIVE: use phenobarbital or propofol**
ECG: sinus tach; QRS >100 ms: TCA; QTc prolongation
--POC glucose
--Acetaminophen & salicylate levels ( mandatory coingestion screen)
--BMP
--CPK if prolonged agitation (Rhabdo)
--Urinalysis
--UDS (limited utility: detects many anticholinergic agents poorly)
Anticholinergic = DRY; sympathomimetic = WET: **check axillae for moisture (key distinguishing exam finding)**
Avoid Class IA/IC antiarrhythmics (procainamide, flecainide) if TCA suspected
Plant ingestions (jimson weed) may have delayed abs from ↓ GI motility: watch 24-48 hrs
Mydriasis may last 12-24 hrs after or sx resolve = !!cant use pupil size to determine resolution!!
Diphenhydramine is dose dependent: mild anticholinergic at low doses: QRS widening, seizures, Rhabdo at high doses
**Always check ECG before giving physostigmine: QRS >100 ms = contraindication**

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.dose: 2-4 mg IV q5-15 min PRN agitation
drugs.notes: Firstline for agitation: controls muscular heat generation, prevents hyperthermia

drugs.name: Physostigmine
drugs.dose: 0.5-1 mg IV slowly over 5 min; may repeat q20 min up to 2 mg total in first hr
drugs.contraindications: TCA ingestion, QRS >100 ms, ↓ HR, AV block, seizure hx, unknown OD
drugs.notes: Reverses central & peripheral effects. If needing >3 doses in 6 hrs, consider infusion 1 mg/hr. Duration shorter than most ingested agents: rebound risk

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.dose: 2 mEq/kg IV bolus, then infusion 150 mEq in 1L D5W at 250 mL/hr
drugs.notes: For QRS >100 ms (TCA sodium channel blockade): goal QRS <120 ms. Can give serial boluses

drugs.name: Activated charcoal
drugs.dose: 1 g/kg PO (max 50 g)
drugs.notes: Most effective within 1-2 hrs of ingestion; anticholinergics delay gastric emptying: may still be effective later

pairs.value: "Blind as bat" (mydriasis), "Mad as hatter" (delirium), "Red as beet" (flushed), "Hot as hare" (hyperthermia), "Dry as bone" (anhidrosis), "Full as flask" (urinary retention)
Blockade of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors: loss of parasympathetic tone: sympathetic dominance
Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor: crosses BBB: reverses both central (delirium) & peripheral (tachycardia, mydriasis) effects
TCAs block fast sodium channels: QRS widening, right axis deviation, Brugada pattern: treat with sodium bicarbonate

sections.title: Tier 1 Management
items: Decontamination: activated charcoal if early (<1-2 hr); whole bowel irrigation for sustained-release CCBs/amlodipine (must be before shock/ileus). Glucagon may not be compatible with bowel irrigation (relaxes GI smooth muscle)
Airway: secure early if deteriorating. Try to achieve hemodynamic stability before intubation to avoid post-intubation hypotension (volume load + epinephrine infusion first)
Vascular access: central access for severe cases (needed for D50W, calcium, vasopressors). Consider arterial line for hemodynamic monitoring
Volume: IV fluids if hypovolemic, but most pts are NOT hypovolemic. Avoid over-resuscitation (volume overload is a major problem in severe cases)

Vasopressors: epinephrine for bradycardia + shock; norepinephrine for vasodilatory shock. Patients may need unusually high doses. No maximum dose of catecholamines. Consider early HIE rather than escalating to extreme vasopressor doses

Glucagon: 5 mg IV over 5 min (may repeat x1). If no improvement after 10 mg: stop. If effective: infuse at effective dose 1-10 mg/hr. Pre-treat with ondansetron. Caution: emesis risk with unprotected airway. Hospital supply may be limited: consider milrinone instead
IV calcium: CaCl 1 g (central) or Ca gluconate 3 g (peripheral) slow push over ≥5 min. Repeat q10-20 min. Target ionized Ca ~2 mM. May improve BP & contractility more than heart rate
Atropine: 1 mg IV q5 min x 1-3 doses (max 3 mg). Unlikely to work in severe CCB OD

HIE: insulin 1 unit/kg bolus then 1 unit/kg/hr. Up-titrate q10-15 min to 1-10 units/kg/hr (>5 units/kg/hr may be excessive). Give D50W 1-2 amps unless glucose >250. Start D50W infusion ~1 mL/kg/hr via central line. Monitor glucose q15-30 min (target 125-250 mg/dL), K+ >3 mM, Mg, Phos

Ionized calcium level (target ~2 mM if giving IV calcium)
Serum lactate: tissue hypoperfusion marker

sections.title: Tier 2 Management
items: Hemodialysis: consider for hydrophilic BBs (nadolol, sotalol, acebutolol, atenolol, timolol). CRRT for renal failure to avoid volume overload
Methylene blue: for refractory vasodilatory shock from CCBs (CCBs ↑ nitric oxide synthesis). Not for cardiogenic shock
VA-ECMO: definitive rescue for refractory cardiogenic shock. Supports pt until drug metabolism occurs. Limited by availability. Contact ECMO center early

Transvenous pacemaker: may help refractory bradycardia with preserved contractility, but results often disappointing. Capturing the myocardium is difficult (myocardial problem, not conduction problem). Loss of atrial kick and uncoordinated contraction may negate benefit of ↑ HR

Lipid emulsion (20%): falling out of favor. Concern that lipid may ↑ drug absorption from intestine. Reasonable for cardiac arrest/periarrest. 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then 0.25 mL/kg/min x 30-60 min. Unlikely to work with hydrophilic BBs. Risks: pancreatitis, ARDS, lab interference, ECMO circuit clotting

pairs.value: Following clinical improvement. In CCB OD, emergence of hypoglycemia may signal recovery
Insulin accumulates & persists hours to days after stopping (especially with renal dysfunction). Can wean rapidly as it auto-tapers. Resume if hemodynamic deterioration
Continue dextrose infusion and adjust based on glucose levels. Do NOT stop dextrose just because insulin was stopped
Watch for hypoglycemia and hyperkalemia/hypokalemia even after insulin is off (rebound hyperkalemia can occur)
Primarily a BB issue (interferes with gluconeogenesis & glycogenolysis). Monitor glucose closely; replete with D50W as needed
BBs: propranolol, acebutolol, betaxolol, carvedilol, oxprenolol, pindolol. Causes QRS widening, monomorphic VT, Brugada pattern. Treat: IV hypertonic bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg (same as TCA OD)
BBs: acebutolol, sotalol. Causes QTc prolongation, torsade de pointes. Treat: IV magnesium 2 g bolus; Mg infusion for torsade. Consider overdrive pacing

drugs.name: Epinephrine
drugs.dose: Start 1 mcg/min, titrate to MAP ≥60; no maximum dose
drugs.notes: Good first-line vasopressor: helps both bradycardia and hypotension. High doses may be needed

drugs.name: Norepinephrine
drugs.dose: Start 0.1-0.5 mcg/kg/min, titrate to MAP
drugs.notes: Preferred for vasodilatory shock (dihydropyridine CCBs, vasodilatory BBs like labetalol, carvedilol)

drugs.name: Calcium chloride 10%
drugs.dose: 1 g IV over ≥5 min via central line; repeat q10-20 min up to 3 g total
drugs.contraindications: Digoxin toxicity (calcium worsens dig toxicity). Causes tissue necrosis if extravasates
drugs.notes: 3x more elemental Ca than gluconate. Target ionized Ca ~2 mM. May need repeat doses q1-2 hr

drugs.name: Calcium gluconate 10%
drugs.dose: 3 g IV over ≥5 min; repeat q10-20 min up to 9 g total
drugs.notes: Preferred without central access. Target ionized Ca ~2 mM

drugs.name: Regular insulin (HIE)
drugs.dose: 1 unit/kg IV bolus, then 1 unit/kg/hr infusion. Up-titrate q10-15 min to max 10 units/kg/hr
drugs.contraindications: Monitor glucose q15-30 min; maintain K+ >3.0 mM
drugs.notes: Most effective therapy for CCB/BB cardiogenic shock. Takes 15-60 min for full effect: START EARLY. Give D50W bolus + infusion. Wean dextrose based on glucose, not insulin

drugs.name: Dextrose 50% (D50W)
drugs.dose: 1-2 amps (50-100 mL) bolus when starting HIE (unless glucose >250). Infusion: ~1 mL/kg/hr via central line
drugs.notes: Essential with HIE. D50W via central preferred to avoid volume overload. Target glucose 125-250 mg/dL

drugs.name: Glucagon
drugs.dose: 5 mg IV bolus over 5 min; may repeat x1 (max test dose 10 mg). Infusion: 1-10 mg/hr
drugs.contraindications: Pheochromocytoma, insulinoma. Caution: unprotected airway (causes emesis)
drugs.notes: Primarily for BB OD. Pre-treat with ondansetron. Short t1/2 (5-7 min): needs infusion. May exhaust pharmacy supply. If glucagon works but supply limited: switch to milrinone

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.dose: 1 mg IV q5 min, max 3 mg cumulative
drugs.notes: Trial is reasonable for bradycardia but unlikely to work in severe CCB/BB OD

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.dose: 1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus
drugs.notes: For QRS widening from Na channel blocking BBs (propranolol, carvedilol). Same approach as TCA OD

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.dose: 2 g IV bolus over 15-20 min; infusion 1-2 g/hr for active torsade
drugs.notes: For QTc prolongation (sotalol, acebutolol). Treat active torsade with Mg infusion + overdrive pacing

drugs.name: Methylene blue
drugs.dose: 1-2 mg/kg IV over 5-30 min; may repeat
drugs.contraindications: G6PD deficiency, serotonergic drugs (serotonin syndrome risk)
drugs.notes: Tier-2 therapy for refractory vasodilatory shock from CCBs. CCBs ↑ nitric oxide synthesis. Not for cardiogenic shock

drugs.name: Lipid emulsion 20%
drugs.dose: 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus (repeat 1-2x if pulseless), then 0.25 mL/kg/min x 30-60 min; max 12.5 mL/kg
drugs.contraindications: Pancreatitis, avoid if ECMO planned (clots circuits)
drugs.notes: Falling out of favor. May worsen absorption. Reasonable in cardiac arrest/periarrest only. Ineffective for hydrophilic BBs

pairs.value: Verapamil, diltiazem: cause myocardial suppression > vasodilation. Early ↓ HR + ↓ BP. Verapamil is most dangerous CCB in overdose
Amlodipine, nifedipine, felodipine: primarily vasodilatory at lower doses (↓ BP with reflex tachycardia). Higher doses lose selectivity and cause bradycardia + vasodilation
Most dangerous BB in OD. Highly lipophilic (crosses BBB: seizures, coma). Na channel blockade: QRS widening, monomorphic VT, Brugada pattern. Severe hypotension
K channel blockade: QTc prolongation + torsade de pointes risk. Bradycardia + QT prolongation synergistically promote torsade. Delayed & prolonged toxicity. Dialyzable
Acebutolol, betaxolol, carvedilol, oxprenolol, pindolol, propranolol: cause QRS widening, monomorphic VT, Brugada pattern. Treat with IV sodium bicarbonate
Betaxolol, carvedilol, labetalol, nebivolol: cause hypotension partly from peripheral vasodilation. May need norepinephrine
Insulin ↑ myocardial inotropy independent of beta-receptors. Most effective for cardiogenic shock from CCB/BB OD. Takes 15-60 min to work: start early, do not wait for other therapies to fail
Increases myocardial cAMP bypassing beta-receptor. Positive inotropic + chronotropic effects. Most useful for BB OD with cardiogenic shock. Short half-life (5-7 min): requires continuous infusion
Also ↑ cAMP bypassing beta-receptor. Consider if glucagon supply is limited. Risk of vasodilation worsening ↓ BP. Renally cleared with long half-life

topics.title: Opioid & Medetomidine Withdrawal
topics.subtitle: Two-track approach: µ-opioid deficit + α2-agonist deficit — fentanyl era, Philadelphia context

sections.title: The First 60 Seconds
items: Airway: airway patent? Look, listen; suction if secretions/blood; jaw thrust if obstructed; call for airway help early
-If Pt looks terrible, can't protect airway: call ICU + anesthesia, then get ready to intubate
Breathing: RR, SpO2(good pleth?), WOB, accessory muscle use, paradoxical breathing, speaking in full sentences?
Start O2 now: NRB 15 L/min if in distress
Rapid O2 escalation if NRB insufficient: HFNC (up to 60 L/min, FiO2 up to 100%) → NIPPV → intubation
Circulation: HR, BP, perfusion; ↓BP, then tension PTX, PE, or cardiogenic shock
Put on cardiac monitor
Check fingerstick glucose.

sections.title: Step 1 — Differentiate: Opioid vs. Medetomidine Withdrawal

pairs.value: Mydriasis, piloerection, rhinorrhea/lacrimation, yawning, diarrhea, diffuse pain/myalgias, craving, restlessness. Substantially improves after adequate opioid agonism. COWS captures this component well.

Rapidly escalating hypertension (SBP >180–240 reported), marked sinus tachycardia (HR >140–180 reported), severe/intractable vomiting, tremor or myoclonic-appearing movements, profuse diaphoresis, anxiety/agitation, waxing-waning or hypoactive mental status. Symptoms out of proportion to classic opioid withdrawal; poor response to escalating opioids despite clear tolerance.

Medetomidine withdrawal begins ~4–6 hours after last exposure and can become dramatic over subsequent hours. Philadelphia original cohort: 91% required ICU care, 83% received and responded to dexmedetomidine.

Bags/day? Bundles/day? (1 bundle = 14 bags) Route (IV, intranasal, smoked)? Administrations per day? Last use? Wakes overnight to use? Prior ICU admission for withdrawal? Prior severe medetomidine withdrawal may predict recurrence better than bag count.

COWS 5–12: Mild. 13–24: Moderate. 25–36: Moderately severe. >36: Severe. COWS is useful for trending but can underestimate severity in fentanyl-era withdrawal; medetomidine autonomic findings inflate it while the sickest hypoactive patients may paradoxically score lower. Do not override the bedside examination.

Do NOT wait for UDS before treating a convincing syndrome. Standard opioid immunoassays frequently miss fentanyl, buprenorphine, and methadone unless specifically ordered. Treat the clinical syndrome.

Alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, stimulant intoxication, serotonin syndrome, NMS, sepsis, thyrotoxicosis, PRES, intracranial pathology, hypoglycemia, DKA, severe electrolyte derangement, acute pain — consider before attributing entirely to withdrawal

pairs.key: Key principle: tolerance tier, not MME conversion
pairs.value: Do NOT convert bags or counterfeit pills to MME. Medetomidine and fentanyl concentrations vary substantially between bags and over time. Use reported use to classify tolerance tier, then titrate against withdrawal, craving, sedation, and respiratory status. Do not document '14 bags = X mg oxycodone.'
Counterfeit pills frequently contain fentanyl, not oxycodone. Treat as fentanyl exposure — do NOT assume 30 mg oxycodone equivalence.

Penn Medicine CAMP estimates one Philadelphia bag may approximate ~300 mg oral oxycodone agonism. This is Philadelphia-specific, cannot be generalized, and explains why 5–10 bags/day produces extreme tolerance. Do not apply this conversion to other cities or drug supplies.
Moderate tolerance. Oxy ER 10–20 mg PO q8h scheduled + Oxy IR 10–15 mg PO q6h PRN
Moderate-high tolerance. Oxy ER 20–30 mg PO q8h scheduled + Oxy IR 15–20 mg PO q6h PRN
High tolerance. Oxy ER 30–40 mg PO q8h scheduled + Oxy IR 20–30 mg PO q6h PRN

Very high tolerance. Oxy ER 40 mg PO q8h scheduled + Oxy IR 30 mg PO q6h PRN. Alternative Penn/EMCrit full-agonist approach: Oxy IR 40 mg PO q4h (increase by 10 mg for persistent COWS >8). Goal COWS ≤5 without sedation.

Start at approximately the 1-bundle tier; titrate from observed rescue requirements at 12–24h rather than extrapolating indefinitely from bag count. Do not write Oxy ER 80–100 mg q8h automatically. Observed opioid requirement during first 12–24h is a safer guide.

pairs.key: <2 bags/day, elderly, critical illness, or organ dysfunction
pairs.value: Use approximately 50% lower starting doses and extend reassessment intervals.

sections.title: Step 3 — Opioid Track: Full-Agonist Framework
items: **Goal:** Treat µ-opioid receptor deficit. Targets — COWS ≤5, craving substantially reduced, no vomiting/diarrhea from opioid withdrawal, patient can sleep, not considering leaving. Do NOT target COWS = 0 at all costs.
**Scheduled baseline (oxy ER):** Provides continuous opioid receptor occupancy. Choose tier from tolerance stratification above. Start scheduled doses and allow meaningful rescue medication.
**Rescue (oxy IR):** Allow q6h PRN doses for withdrawal symptoms, craving, or COWS >8 attributable to opioid component. Rescue doses at the same tier as the scheduled dose (see table above).

**IV hydromorphone — floor indication:** Reserve for severe breakthrough symptoms despite oral rescue, active vomiting preventing PO, or severe acute pain. Start 1–2 mg IV q2h PRN; upward titrate in clearly extremely tolerant patients who remain awake, tachypneic rather than hypoventilating, and objectively withdrawing. Reassess sedation and RR after each dose.

**IV hydromorphone — ICU/cannot tolerate PO:** Penn/EMCrit ICU pathway: hydromorphone 4 mg IV q2h; for COWS >8, increase by 1–2 mg as frequently as every 30 minutes during active titration. This is an ICU/high-tolerance pathway — do NOT copy to opioid-naïve or uncertain-tolerance patients.
**Hold for:** New somnolence, difficult arousal, slurred speech, falling RR, new hypoxemia, miosis + sedation, or any sign of opioid intoxication.

**Alternative — methadone-based:** Methadone 20–40 mg PO day 1; reassess 2–4h before substantial redosing (methadone stacks). QTc monitoring when: known prolonged QT, high doses, multiple QT-prolonging drugs. See Methadone Pathway section.

sections.title: Opioid Track: 24-Hour Titration & Upward Adjustment
items: Reassess after each dose: COWS components specific to opioid withdrawal, craving, pain, RR, SpO2, sedation, pupils, ability to converse normally.

At ~24 hours: calculate total oxycodone IR actually required. If patient was never sedated and remained significantly symptomatic, incorporate approximately 50–75% of the prior day's effective rescue requirement into the next day's scheduled opioid.

Example: Oxy ER 40 mg q8h = 120 mg/day baseline. Patient required four oxy IR 30 mg doses (+120 mg). Total observed = 240 mg/day. Next day: Oxy ER 50–60 mg q8h + Oxy IR 20–30 mg q6h PRN, then reassess again.
Do NOT automatically schedule all of yesterday's total — step titrate with preserved breakthrough and frequent reassessment.

**Critical checkpoint:** Once pain is controlled, pupillary/GI opioid findings have improved, and craving is substantially improved — but patient remains hypertensive (BP 200/120), tachycardic, vomiting, tremulous, sweaty, or encephalopathic — STOP escalating opioids. That remaining syndrome is medetomidine withdrawal. Intensify alpha-2 replacement instead.

pairs.value: Medetomidine creates α2-adrenergic receptor dependence. Withdrawal = α2-deficiency syndrome with autonomic storm. Replace the missing α2 agonism with clonidine → tizanidine → clonidine patch, escalating to IV dexmedetomidine when oral therapy cannot keep up. Do not endlessly escalate opioids for a primarily α2-deficiency problem.

Clonidine 0.2 mg PO q4h for clear autonomic withdrawal. With particularly severe HTN/tachycardia and adequate BP reserve: 0.3 mg PO q4–6h. Hold for SBP <100, MAP <65, HR <55–60, symptomatic hypotension, or new excessive sedation.
Do NOT abruptly stop high-dose clonidine after several days of therapy — patient can develop clonidine withdrawal superimposed on medetomidine withdrawal. Taper gradually.

Add when clonidine alone does not provide enough α2 coverage. Tizanidine 4 mg PO q8h scheduled (can give 2–4 mg PRN). PDPH guidance: 2–4 mg q6–8h PRN. Watch: sedation, hypotension, bradycardia, LFTs (prolonged use), QTc, drug interactions — strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine) dramatically increase tizanidine levels.

For prolonged courses: clonidine patch 0.1–0.3 mg/day (change q7 days). Onset is slow (~18–24h) — useless as acute rescue but valuable as background α2 coverage and for bridging off dexmedetomidine. Place early for anticipated prolonged withdrawal. Particularly useful during Precedex de-escalation — 'Precedex extinguishes the storm; clonidine patch/tizanidine prevent the storm from returning when Precedex disappears.'
Clonidine 0.2 mg PO q4h + Tizanidine 2–4 mg PO q6–8h PRN
Clonidine 0.3 mg PO q4–6h (if hemodynamics allow) + Tizanidine 4 mg q6–8h + Consider clonidine patch early

Do not spend 8 hours cycling through clonidine → Ativan → Haldol → more Dilaudid → more clonidine → more oxycodone while the patient remains BP 220/130 and vomiting. Escalate to ICU and dexmedetomidine early.

sections.title: Step 5 — When to Escalate to ICU (Precedex Triggers)
items: **Escalate early for any of:** SBP ≥180 or DBP ≥120 despite initial therapy; rapidly rising BP/HR not responding to oral α2 therapy
Intractable vomiting preventing oral α2 therapy (loss of oral route = floor strategy failing)
Waxing/waning consciousness or severely hypoactive mental status
Severe agitation not controlled with oral medications
Chest pain; troponin elevation; PRES symptoms (headache, visual changes, seizure)
QTc >500 ms with multiple necessary QT-prolonging agents
Severe metabolic abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, severe acidosis)
Severe symptoms not materially improving within ~4–6 hours of adequate floor therapy
Philadelphia 2026 cohort context: 91% of severe medetomidine withdrawal cases required ICU care — have a low threshold in this population.

sections.title: Dexmedetomidine (Precedex) Protocol & Combination Strategy
items: **Rationale:** Dexmedetomidine is not merely a sedative in this context — it is pharmacologically replacing the missing α2 agonist. This distinguishes it from benzos or antipsychotics in this syndrome.
**Starting dose:** Dexmedetomidine 0.5 mcg/kg/hr IV.

**Titration (Penn ICU protocol):** Increase by up to 0.4 mcg/kg/hr every ~20 minutes. Nurse-driven ceiling: 1.5 mcg/kg/hr. Provider-directed for refractory cases: up to 2.5 mcg/kg/hr. Titrate to: control severe autonomic symptoms, SBP <160 (Penn target), improvement in vomiting/tremor, clinically appropriate RASS. 2026 review: most require ~24–72h infusion.

**Loading bolus:** Penn permits 0.5–1 mcg/kg IV in selected rapidly deteriorating patients with adequate hemodynamic reserve. Do NOT routinely bolus — dramatic bradycardia/hypotension can follow. Restrict to providers with clear indication and monitoring in place.
**Hold/start cautiously if:** HR <50, MAP <65, second/third-degree AV block without pacing, or significant evolving bradycardia.
**Once on dexmedetomidine:** Avoid blindly continuing escalating oral clonidine if BP/HR are falling — risk of additive hypotension/bradycardia.

**Coming off Precedex (de-escalation):** Restart/continue clonidine + tizanidine ± clonidine patch, then taper dexmedetomidine. Overlapping oral/transdermal α2 agonists during de-escalation prevents rebound. The 2026 review specifically supports this overlap strategy.
**Discharge planning:** Get clonidine down to no more than 0.3 mg PO TID before community discharge (PDPH recommendation). Gradual taper with close BP follow-up.

sections.title: Buprenorphine Pathway (When Patient Wants MOUD)
items: **Advantages:** Powerful withdrawal and craving suppression, lower respiratory depression risk, no X-waiver required, prescribable at discharge, straightforward linkage to outpatient treatment.

**Induction timing — fentanyl era:** Do NOT rely on '12 hours since last use.' Wait for convincing objective withdrawal. SAMHSA recommends COWS >12. Note: severe medetomidine withdrawal can precede classic fentanyl withdrawal — a high early COWS should not automatically trigger conventional buprenorphine induction if the picture is predominantly autonomic.

**Caution in medetomidine withdrawal:** If the patient has not yet been adequately treated for the α2-deficiency component, buprenorphine induction timing requires extra care. Consult addiction medicine when uncertain.
**Conservative start:** Buprenorphine/naloxone 2–4 mg SL → reassess 30–60 min → additional 4–8 mg. Repeat until withdrawal and craving controlled.

**High fentanyl tolerance, clearly in withdrawal:** Buprenorphine 8–16 mg SL initially → reassess 30–60 min → additional 8–16 mg if still withdrawing. Common day-1 total: 24–32 mg. ASAM: rapid escalation to 24–32 mg/day recognized for high-potency synthetic opioid users. FDA labeling updated — 24 mg is no longer an absolute daily maximum.

sections.title: Precipitated Withdrawal — Recognition & Treatment
items: **Classic scenario:** Within 15–60 min of buprenorphine: abrupt dramatic worsening — vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, piloerection, agitation, myalgias, tachycardia, severe distress.
**Do not stop buprenorphine.** Do not conclude it failed. The most effective treatment is usually more buprenorphine.
**ASAM:** If <16 mg given, rapidly increase toward 24–32 mg total. Published experience up to 64 mg (not routine).
**Refractory precipitated withdrawal (ASAM options):** High-affinity full agonist opioid; dexmedetomidine; ketamine 0.3 mg/kg IV over 10–15 min; targeted benzodiazepine use; additional buprenorphine.

sections.title: Low-Dose Buprenorphine / Microinduction
items: **Best indications:** Daily fentanyl use; prior precipitated withdrawal; significant acute pain; patient currently on full agonists; methadone-to-buprenorphine transitions.
**Strategy:** Full agonists are continued while small buprenorphine doses gradually occupy receptors — avoiding precipitated withdrawal.
**Penn inpatient protocol (example):** Day 1: buccal buprenorphine 300 mcg q4h OR 150 mcg q3h. Day 2: buprenorphine/naloxone 2 mg SL q6h. Day 3: 4 mg SL q6h. Day 4: 16–24 mg/day.
Full agonists continue through induction and are tapered once meaningful buprenorphine receptor occupancy is achieved. Institutional protocols vary.

sections.title: Methadone Pathway
items: **Indications:** Patient wants methadone maintenance; very heavy fentanyl exposure; prior precipitated buprenorphine withdrawal; significant acute pain requiring full agonism; buprenorphine induction has repeatedly failed.

**Standard initiation:** Methadone 20–30 mg PO day 1 → reassess 2–4h → additional 10 mg if clearly withdrawing and awake. Goal: ~30–40 mg day 1 for moderate tolerance; 40–60 mg for heavy fentanyl tolerance (with appropriate monitoring).

**Safety pearl — methadone stacks:** Withdrawal improves quickly; methadone toxicity accumulates slowly. Do NOT redose every 60 minutes because the patient is still miserable. Peak effect delayed; half-life far exceeds initial subjective effect.
**Hold for:** New somnolence, difficult arousal, slurred speech, falling RR, new hypoxemia, miosis + sedation.

**QTc monitoring:** Check ECG when known prolonged QT, high doses, structural heart disease, hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, multiple QT-prolonging drugs, or medetomidine-related autonomic instability. QTc >500 ms warrants specialty input.

pairs.value: Once oral medications stop staying down, the entire floor management strategy collapses — patient cannot receive oral opioids, oral α2 agonists, or buprenorphine. Treat vomiting aggressively and early.

Ondansetron may perform poorly in established medetomidine withdrawal. Penn experience and current reviews favor dopamine antagonists: prochlorperazine 10 mg IV q8h PRN, or olanzapine 5–10 mg PO/IV/IM. Penn ICU: olanzapine 10 mg ×1, then 5 mg qHS. Check QTc and cumulative dopamine-antagonist exposure before prescribing.
Is this severe asymptomatic withdrawal hypertension, or hypertensive emergency? If no end-organ injury — treating the underlying α2 deficit is often the most physiologic treatment (dexmedetomidine).

pairs.key: If hypertensive emergency with end-organ injury
pairs.value: PRES, ACS/myocardial injury, pulmonary edema, aortic syndrome, or encephalopathy attributable to BP — treat concurrently with: nicardipine infusion, esmolol infusion, IV labetalol, or IV hydralazine. Do not normalize BP abruptly solely because it looks alarming.

sections.title: Still Refractory — Reassess Diagnosis First
items: **Before adding more medications, check:** Is this alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal?
Is the patient stimulant-intoxicated (co-use of cocaine, methamphetamine)?
Sepsis, thyrotoxicosis, PRES, intracranial pathology?
Hypoglycemia, DKA, severe electrolyte derangement?
Is there untreated acute pain on top of withdrawal?
Did buprenorphine precipitate withdrawal — and has enough additional buprenorphine been given?
Is akathisia from an antiemetic or antipsychotic being mistaken for worsening withdrawal?
Are you substantially underdosing a patient with massive fentanyl tolerance?
Did the patient vomit the oral medication?
Have you asked the patient directly whether the medication is actually helping?

**If diagnosis remains medetomidine withdrawal and patient is on adequate opioid + oral α2 therapy — add ketamine:** Penn/EMCrit: ketamine infusion 0.1–0.5 mg/kg/hr IV; or if PO feasible: 1.5–3 mg/kg/day divided q6h. Ketamine is an adjunct to α2 agonism, not a replacement.

sections.title: Monitoring & Lab Order Set (Severe Withdrawal)
items: **Monitoring:** Telemetry, continuous pulse oximetry, vitals q1h initially, COWS q4h (do not rely on COWS alone), RASS while on dexmedetomidine, strict I/O if severe vomiting

**Labs:** CBC, CMP, Mg, Phos, VBG/ABG if ill, lactate, CK if significant tremor/agitation, troponin if severe tachycardia/HTN/chest pain, ECG/QTc, UDS including fentanyl when available, EtOH level, targeted sedative testing based on history
**Aggressively replace:** K+ >4.0, Mg >2.0 — particularly with vomiting, methadone exposure, antipsychotics, or prolonged QT

drugs.name: Clonidine
drugs.contraindications: Hold for SBP <100, MAP <65, HR <55–60, symptomatic orthostasis. Taper gradually — do not stop abruptly after multi-day high-dose use.
drugs.notes: First-line α2 replacement for medetomidine withdrawal. 0.2 mg q4h initial; 0.3 mg q4–6h for severe autonomic symptoms with adequate BP reserve.

drugs.name: Tizanidine
drugs.dose: 2–4 mg PO q6–8h PRN; can schedule 4 mg q8h
drugs.contraindications: Watch QTc, sedation, hypotension, bradycardia. Strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine) dramatically increase tizanidine levels — major interaction.
drugs.notes: Adjunct α2 agonist when clonidine alone insufficient. Add when oral clonidine at 0.2–0.3 mg q4h still not controlling autonomic symptoms.

drugs.name: Clonidine patch
drugs.dose: 0.1–0.3 mg/24h; change q7 days
drugs.contraindications: Slow onset (18–24h) — not for acute rescue
drugs.notes: Use for prolonged withdrawal or during Precedex de-escalation. Provides stable background α2 coverage; prevents rebound when dexmedetomidine is tapered.

drugs.name: Dexmedetomidine
drugs.dose: Start 0.5 mcg/kg/hr IV; titrate by 0.4 mcg/kg/hr q20min; usual ceiling 1.5 mcg/kg/hr; refractory up to 2.5 mcg/kg/hr
drugs.contraindications: HR <50, MAP <65, 2nd/3rd-degree AV block without pacing. Loading bolus (0.5–1 mcg/kg) only in selected patients with adequate hemodynamic reserve — risk of severe bradycardia/hypotension.
drugs.notes: Pharmacologically replacing missing α2 agonism, not just sedating. Most patients require 24–72h infusion. Overlap oral α2 agonists before weaning.

drugs.name: Ondansetron
drugs.dose: 4–8 mg PO/IV q6–8h PRN
drugs.contraindications: QTc prolongation — check QTc; may underperform in medetomidine withdrawal
drugs.notes: First-line antiemetic for opioid-component nausea; may be insufficient in established medetomidine withdrawal

drugs.name: Prochlorperazine
drugs.dose: 10 mg IV q8h PRN
drugs.contraindications: QTc, EPS, akathisia (can mimic worsening withdrawal), avoid if NMS suspected
drugs.notes: Preferred antiemetic in medetomidine withdrawal (dopamine antagonist); monitor QTc and cumulative dopamine-antagonist load

drugs.name: Olanzapine
drugs.dose: 5–10 mg PO/IV/IM; Penn ICU: 10 mg ×1, then 5 mg qHS
drugs.contraindications: QTc prolongation; avoid concurrent IV benzodiazepines
drugs.notes: For refractory vomiting and agitation in medetomidine withdrawal; check QTc and cumulative dopamine-antagonist exposure

drugs.name: Loperamide
drugs.dose: 2 mg PO q2h PRN, max 16 mg/day
drugs.contraindications: Do not exceed max; do not use in toxic megacolon
drugs.notes: For diarrhea from opioid withdrawal component

drugs.name: Hydroxyzine
drugs.dose: 25–50 mg PO q6h PRN
drugs.notes: For anxiety/agitation adjunct

drugs.name: Acetaminophen
drugs.notes: For myalgias and pain

drugs.name: Ketamine (refractory)
drugs.dose: Infusion 0.1–0.5 mg/kg/hr IV; or PO 1.5–3 mg/kg/day divided q6h
drugs.notes: Adjunct for refractory medetomidine withdrawal or precipitated buprenorphine withdrawal; not a replacement for α2 agonism

drugs.name: Methadone (induction)
drugs.dose: 20–30 mg PO day 1; titrate 10 mg increments q2–4h to COWS <6 without sedation
drugs.contraindications: QTc >500 ms, significant co-sedation, severe respiratory compromise. Does NOT redose q60min — methadone stacks.
drugs.notes: Peak effect 2–4h. Continuous monitoring for first 24h. Alternative opioid track when patient wants methadone maintenance.

drugs.name: Buprenorphine/naloxone
drugs.dose: 2–8 mg SL to start; titrate to 16–32 mg day 1 for high fentanyl tolerance
drugs.contraindications: Do not give until convincing objective withdrawal present (COWS >8–12 minimum, >12 for fentanyl); extra caution in medetomidine withdrawal where induction timing is complex
drugs.notes: No X-waiver required. 24 mg no longer absolute daily maximum (updated FDA labeling).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: **Treating the medetomidine component by endlessly escalating opioids:** Once adequate µ-opioid agonism has been achieved and the patient is still in autonomic storm, more hydromorphone or oxycodone does not fix α2 deficiency.

**Clonidine-only treatment for the α2 component:** May reduce HR and diaphoresis while patient remains profoundly symptomatic — escalate to tizanidine and then dexmedetomidine when oral α2 therapy is failing.
**Waiting too long for ICU escalation:** Severe medetomidine withdrawal can involve SBP >240, HR >180. If oral medications cannot keep up and vomiting is preventing oral therapy, escalate early.
**Assuming COWS accurately captures the whole syndrome:** Medetomidine autonomic findings inflate COWS; the sickest hypoactive patients may score paradoxically lower.
**Oxycodone 5 mg PRN for a 10-bag/day fentanyl user:** Pharmacologically irrelevant relative to their tolerance.
**Treating the COWS number rather than the patient:** COWS was not designed for today's fentanyl-medetomidine drug supply.
**Waiting for the urine tox before treating:** Treatment is clinical.
**Assuming counterfeit M30 = oxycodone 30 mg:** Treat as fentanyl exposure.
**Stopping buprenorphine when precipitated withdrawal occurs:** Give more buprenorphine.
**Giving methadone every hour because the patient still feels bad:** Methadone stacks — respect its delayed peak.
**Abruptly stopping high-dose clonidine after several days:** Can precipitate clonidine withdrawal superimposed on medetomidine withdrawal.
**Calling extreme hypertension 'just opioid withdrawal':** In 2026 Philadelphia/mid-Atlantic, think medetomidine α2 deficiency first.

sections.title: Bedside Shorthand — One-Bundle/Day Patient
items: **Initial orders:** Oxycodone ER 40 mg PO q8h scheduled + Oxycodone IR 30 mg PO q6h PRN (withdrawal/craving/COWS >8) + Hydromorphone 1–2 mg IV q2h PRN severe breakthrough
**Alpha-2 from the start:** Clonidine 0.2 mg PO q4h + Tizanidine 4 mg PO q8h PRN
**Aggressive antiemetics:** Prochlorperazine 10 mg IV q8h PRN or olanzapine 5 mg PO qHS; check QTc
**Telemetry, frequent BP/HR, COWS q4h**

**If after adequate opioid treatment the patient still has HR 145, BP 210/120, repeated emesis, tremor, or encephalopathy:** Do not double the Dilaudid. Escalate to ICU. Start dexmedetomidine 0.5 mcg/kg/hr → rapidly titrate to symptom control (usual ceiling 1.5, refractory up to 2.5 mcg/kg/hr).
**Coming off dexmedetomidine:** Continue/restart clonidine ± tizanidine ± clonidine patch, then taper Precedex. Overlap prevents rebound storm.

pairs.value: Once awake and objectively withdrawing, high-dose buprenorphine initiation can be highly effective rather than waiting hours.
Continue or initiate methadone or buprenorphine. Avoid abstinence-only withdrawal strategy. Involve OB and Addiction Medicine early.
Buprenorphine and methadone generally perform well. Avoid morphine and codeine. Hydromorphone preferable to morphine for short-acting use, though metabolites may accumulate in ESRD.
Reduce initial agonist doses by ~50% and extend reassessment intervals. Clonidine can cause pronounced hypotension — start low.
May simultaneously have enormous tolerance and limited respiratory reserve. Lower incremental doses, frequent sedation checks, continuous SpO2, consider capnography at high risk.

Maintenance MOUD does not provide adequate analgesia. For methadone: continue maintenance + split dosing BID/TID + short-acting opioid for pain. For buprenorphine: divide total dose q6–8h + acetaminophen/NSAIDs/regional ± full agonist if needed. Do NOT stop buprenorphine.
